name: Ulna
func: The forearm bone on the little-finger side. It forms the main hinge of the elbow with the humerus and stays fairly still while the radius rotates around it.

levels.kid:
Your forearm has two bones. The one on your **little-finger side** is called the **ulna**.

Bend your elbow and feel the pointy bump at the back. That's the top of your ulna! When you lean on a table with your elbows, you're leaning on your ulnas.

The ulna is the bone that makes your **elbow hinge**. It hooks around the end of your upper-arm bone like a wrench grabbing a bolt, so your arm can bend and straighten but not twist sideways at the elbow.

While your other forearm bone, the radius, spins around to flip your hand over, the ulna mostly stays still and steady, like the post a gate swings on.

You can feel a little bump on the outside of your wrist near your little finger. That's the bottom of your ulna!
levels.hs:
The **ulna** is the **medial** bone of the forearm, on the **little-finger side**, lying parallel to the **radius** and joined to it by the **interosseous membrane**. It is longer than the radius and is the main bone of the **elbow**, while the radius is the main bone of the wrist.

**Upper end**: a large hook-shaped part. The **olecranon** is the bony point of the elbow at the back, where the **triceps** attaches. In front is the **coronoid process**, and between them a deep, C-shaped **trochlear notch** that grips the trochlea of the humerus to form a strong **hinge joint**. On the side, the **radial notch** holds the head of the radius. The **brachialis** muscle attaches just below the coronoid.

**Shaft**: triangular in cross-section with a sharp edge facing the radius. Its back border can be felt all the way along the forearm under the skin.

**Lower end**: small. The rounded **head of the ulna** forms a joint with the radius (the distal radioulnar joint), and the pointed **ulnar styloid process** sticks down on the little-finger side. A pad of cartilage separates the ulna from the wrist bones.
levels.college:
**Proximal ulna**: the **olecranon** (triceps insertion, subcutaneous **olecranon bursa** over it); the **coronoid process** (brachialis insertion at the **ulnar tuberosity**, and the **sublime tubercle** on its medial side, which anchors the anterior band of the **ulnar collateral ligament**, the key stabiliser against valgus stress, as in throwing); the **supinator crest** below the radial notch for the supinator muscle.

**Elbow stability**: the trochlear notch's deep congruence with the trochlea, the **coronoid** (a buttress against posterior dislocation) and the collateral ligaments make the humeroulnar joint one of the most stable joints in the body.

**Distal ulna**: the head articulates with the **ulnar notch** of the radius at the **distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ)**. The **triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC)**, attaching to the base of the ulnar styloid and the **fovea**, stabilises the DRUJ and cushions the ulnar wrist. The **extensor carpi ulnaris** tendon runs in a groove beside the styloid.

**Relations**: the **ulnar nerve** passes behind the medial epicondyle, then enters the forearm between the two heads of **flexor carpi ulnaris** (the **cubital tunnel**) and runs along the ulna with the **ulnar artery** to the wrist, where both pass through **Guyon's canal** (between the pisiform and hook of hamate) into the hand. Flexor digitorum profundus arises from the front of the shaft.

In a dry skeleton, a simple rule: the ulna is big at the elbow and small at the wrist; the radius is the opposite.
levels.phd:
The ulna and radius emerge from the same limb-bud **zeugopod** condensation. Anteroposterior identity is set by **Sonic hedgehog (SHH)** from the posterior **zone of polarising activity**: the ulna is a posterior (postaxial) element, and its formation requires SHH. In mouse Shh knockouts, the zeugopod forms a single bone, and in humans postaxial defects such as **ulnar hypoplasia** with missing little-finger-side digits are linked to **TBX3** mutations.

The proximal ulna ossifies from the shaft's primary centre plus an **olecranon** secondary centre that appears around age 9–11 and may consist of two parts, which can mimic a fracture on X-ray. Its **trochlear notch** often has a bare, cartilage-free transverse strip, a normal finding.

**Elbow biomechanics**: the humeroulnar joint carries a large share of axial load in extension, while the radiocapitellar joint carries more as the forearm pronates. During overhead throwing, valgus torque at the elbow approaches the failure strength of the ulnar collateral ligament, so dynamic stabilisation by **flexor-pronator** muscles is crucial. This explains the epidemic of UCL tears in young pitchers and the large research effort around pitch counts and throwing mechanics.

The **ulnar nerve** is uniquely vulnerable at the elbow: during flexion, the cubital tunnel's volume falls and pressure in it rises several-fold while the nerve stretches by several millimetres, contributing to **cubital tunnel syndrome**, the second most common nerve entrapment after carpal tunnel.
levels.expert:
**Fractures**:
- **Olecranon fractures** follow falls on the elbow; the triceps pulls the fragment away, so most displaced ones need **tension-band wiring** or plating.
- **Monteggia fracture-dislocation**: a fracture of the proximal ulna **with dislocation of the radial head**. The radial head dislocation is easily missed; on every elbow X-ray, a line through the radial neck should point to the capitellum (**radiocapitellar line**).
- **Nightstick fracture**: an isolated ulnar shaft fracture from a direct blow when raising the arm in defence.
- **Coronoid fractures** with radial head fractures and elbow dislocation form the "**terrible triad**".

**Ulnar nerve** problems: **cubital tunnel syndrome** causes numbness of the little finger and half the ring finger and weakness of the hand's small muscles. Signs: **Froment's sign** (flexing the thumb tip to pinch paper because adductor pollicis is weak), **Wartenberg's sign** (little finger drifts out) and **clawing** of the ring and little fingers (the **ulnar paradox**: lower lesions claw more because FDP is spared). Diagnosis uses **nerve conduction studies** and sometimes ultrasound. Treatment in general includes avoiding prolonged elbow flexion and night splinting, then surgical **decompression** or **anterior transposition** of the nerve, procedures done by hand surgeons and neurosurgeons.

**Ulnar collateral ligament** tears in throwers are reconstructed with a tendon graft (**Tommy John surgery**).

**Wrist**: **ulnar impaction syndrome** from positive ulnar variance and **TFCC tears** cause ulnar-sided wrist pain, assessed with MRI or arthroscopy. **Olecranon bursitis** ("student's elbow") is a fluid swelling over the bony point, sometimes infected.

keyPoints: Medial (little-finger side) forearm bone; main bone of the elbow
Olecranon = elbow point (triceps); coronoid + trochlear notch grip the humerus
Head at the wrist meets the radius at the DRUJ, cushioned by the TFCC
Ulnar nerve: cubital tunnel at the elbow, Guyon's canal at the wrist
Monteggia = ulna fracture + radial head dislocation

test.q: The bony point of the elbow that you lean on is the:
test.explain: The olecranon of the ulna receives the triceps tendon.

test.q: A Monteggia injury is a fracture of the ulna with:
test.explain: Monteggia: ulna broken, radial head dislocated.

test.q: Pinching paper by bending the thumb tip because adductor pollicis is weak is ______ sign.
test.explain: Froment's sign indicates ulnar nerve weakness.

test.q: Which ligament complex stabilises the distal radioulnar joint?
test.explain: The TFCC attaches to the ulnar styloid base and fovea.

test.q: The tunnel at the wrist between the pisiform and hook of hamate carrying the ulnar nerve is ______ canal.
test.explain: Compression here affects the hand's ulnar nerve branches.
